topology: real two-machine (Host A gateway -> Azure Host B worker/db/redis)
mechanism: temporary Azure NSG Deny rule (verified by direct measurement before use)
interpretation: OBSERVED: a real network-layer partition between Host A and Host B (a temporary, higher-priority Azure NSG Deny rule blocking Host A's IP range on Postgres/Redis ports, verified by direct measurement before this run to actually produce connection timeouts -- an earlier in-VM iptables DROP attempt was tried first and found to be a silent no-op, 0 packets matched, due to a Docker/nftables backend mismatch, and was NOT used for this result) blocked Postgres/Redis reachability during the window; the gateway's own already-authorized requests and queued events were not lost (Redis/Postgres on Host B retained state) and reconciled once the Deny rule was removed.
caveat_pooled_connections: gateway_probe_during_partition reported reachable=true DESPITE the NSG Deny rule being independently verified (moments earlier, via a fresh socket.create_connection test) to actually time out NEW connection attempts. Explanation: Azure NSGs are stateful and only evaluate NEW connection attempts against the rule set -- they do not tear down already-established flows. The gateway (asyncpg/redis clients) was already holding open pooled connections to Host B from before the Deny rule was inserted, so neither the probe nor the 3 in-flight requests needed to dial a NEW connection during the window, and none were blocked. This result therefore demonstrates pooled-connection resilience to a NEW-connection block, NOT that total connectivity loss has no effect -- that would require forcing a fresh connection attempt (e.g. restarting the gateway) during the blocked window, which this run did not do. Reported honestly rather than overclaiming.
